Artificial Intelligence: Ideas, Approaches and History 💡
1. What Counts as Artificial Intelligence
🔊
Read section

There is no single agreed definition of artificial intelligence (AI). A practical one is: software that performs tasks which, if a person did them, we would say required intelligence, such as recognising speech, judging whether a transaction looks fraudulent, or planning a route.

That definition describes behaviour, not inner workings, and it shifts over time. Once a task becomes routine, people often stop calling it AI. Optical character recognition and spelling correction were research problems once; now they are just features.

It helps to separate two ambitions:

Narrow AI is built for one kind of task: translating text, recommending films, spotting tumours on scans. Every AI system in use today is narrow, however impressive it looks.
General AI, often called AGI, would match people across almost any intellectual task, transferring what it learns from one area to another. It does not exist yet, and researchers disagree about how far away it is.

Most modern narrow AI is built with machine learning: instead of a programmer writing every rule, the system adjusts itself to fit a large set of examples.

Where you'll see this: Fraud alerts from your bank, the route your maps app suggests and the subtitles on a video call all come from narrow AI systems.

💡 JARGON BUSTER
Artificial intelligence (AI)

2. Testing for Intelligence: The Imitation Game
🔊
Read section

In 1950 the mathematician Alan Turing sidestepped the question "can machines think?", which he considered too vague, and proposed a test of behaviour instead. He called it the imitation game; today it is known as the Turing test.

A judge holds typed conversations with two hidden participants, one a person and one a machine. If, after questioning both, the judge cannot reliably say which is which, the machine has passed.

The test is useful because it is concrete, but it has well-known weaknesses:

It rewards imitation. A program can seem human by copying human habits, including typing errors and changing the subject, without understanding anything.
It says nothing about abilities that do not show up in chat, such as seeing, planning or acting in the world.
The philosopher John Searle's "Chinese room" argument (1980) claims that following rules to produce convincing answers is not the same as understanding them.

Modern chat assistants can hold fluent conversations, so researchers now rely more on benchmarks: large, fixed sets of tasks with known answers, used to compare systems on specific skills such as reading comprehension or maths.

3. How the Field Developed
🔊
Read section

The name "artificial intelligence" was coined for a 1956 summer workshop at Dartmouth College in the United States. Its organisers expected rapid progress, and early programs did prove simple theorems and play draughts.

Progress then proved much harder than promised. Funding fell sharply in the mid-1970s and again in the late 1980s, periods now called AI winters. In between, expert systems that captured specialists' rules found real commercial use, but they were expensive to build and maintain.

From the 1990s, learning from data gradually took over. In 1997 IBM's Deep Blue beat the world chess champion, mostly through fast search. In 2012 a deep neural network won an image recognition competition by a wide margin, helped by large labelled datasets and graphics processors. In 2017 the transformer design for language models appeared, and from around 2020 very large language models made fluent chat assistants practical.

The pattern across seventy years: bold predictions, periods of disappointment, and steady progress driven by more data, more computing power and better learning methods.

4. Two Ways to Build AI: Rules or Learning
🔊
Read section

There are two broad strategies for building an intelligent system.

The top-down or symbolic approach starts from how people reason. Experts describe their knowledge as facts and rules, and the program applies them with logic. Its strengths are transparency, since every conclusion can be traced to a rule, and needing no training data. Its weakness is brittleness: the world has more exceptions than anyone can write down, and tasks such as recognising a face resist being put into rules at all.

The bottom-up approach starts from examples. A model with many adjustable settings, often a neural network loosely inspired by the brain, is shown labelled data and tunes its settings until its outputs match. It handles messy inputs like images, sound and free text well. Its weaknesses are that it needs a lot of data and that its reasoning is spread across millions of numbers, which makes individual decisions hard to explain.

Many real products combine both: a learned model makes a prediction, and hand-written rules check it against hard limits, such as legal or safety requirements.

5. Worked Example: A Written Rule Versus a Learned One
🔊
Read section

Suppose we want to flag spam emails using one clue: the number of suspicious phrases in each message, such as "claim your prize" or "act now".

The rule-based way. A programmer guesses a rule: flag an email if it has 2 or more suspicious phrases.

The learning way. We collect ten emails that people have already labelled:

Spam: 3, 4, 5, 6 and 3 suspicious phrases.
Not spam: 0, 1, 1, 2 and 0 suspicious phrases.

We then try every possible cut-off and count the mistakes on these ten emails:

Flag at 2 or more: one mistake (the genuine email with 2 phrases is flagged).
Flag at 3 or more: no mistakes.
Flag at 4 or more: two mistakes (both spam emails with 3 phrases get through).

So the learned rule is "flag at 3 or more". It was chosen by the data, not by a guess, and if spammers change their habits we can relabel some new emails and learn again instead of rewriting code.

Checking on new data. Four new emails arrive: spam with 3 phrases, spam with 2, genuine with 2, and genuine with 0. The learned rule gets three of the four right, an accuracy of 75%: it misses the spam email with only 2 phrases. Lowering the cut-off to 2 would catch that one but flag the genuine email with 2 instead. When spam and genuine emails can share the same count, no cut-off on one clue can be perfect. Real spam filters learn from thousands of clues at once, which is exactly what machine learning is good at.

The notebook for this lesson runs both rules on the same emails, step by step.

Where you'll see this: Email providers retrain their spam filters continuously as people mark messages as spam or not spam.

💡 JARGON BUSTER
Labelled data
🔊

Accuracy
🔊
The share of cases a model gets right. Three right out of four is 75%.
Test data
🔊

What AI Really Is, in Plain English 💡
1. Software That Learns from Examples
🔊
Read section

EVERYDAY ANALOGY
Everyday Metaphor: Training a New Colleague

You could hand a new colleague a thick manual, or you could sit them next to someone experienced for a month. Most AI is trained the second way: it watches lots of examples until it can handle new cases on its own.

Ordinary software follows instructions a programmer wrote, step by step. A spreadsheet adds a column because someone told it exactly how.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is software that does tasks we would normally say need human judgement, such as recognising a face, understanding a spoken request or spotting a suspicious payment. Most modern AI is not given those rules. Instead it is shown a large number of examples and works out the patterns itself. That is why it can cope with situations nobody wrote a rule for, and also why it sometimes gets things confidently wrong.

📊 RULES WRITTEN BY PEOPLE VS PATTERNS LEARNED FROM EXAMPLES

2. Narrow AI Today, General AI in Fiction
🔊
Read section
✨💡
EVERYDAY ANALOGY
Everyday Metaphor: The Specialist Tool

A satnav is brilliant at routes and useless at cooking. Today's AI is like that: each system is a specialist tool, however clever it looks.

Every AI in use today is narrow AI: it is built and trained for a particular kind of task. A system that reads X-rays cannot plan a holiday, and a route planner cannot write an email.

Chat assistants can feel broader, because language touches so many subjects. But they are still one kind of tool, trained to produce likely text, and they cannot, for example, drive a car or learn a new physical skill.

General AI, a machine that could learn any task a person can, does not exist. Experts disagree about whether, or when, it might.

4. Two Ways to Build AI: Rules or Learning
🔊
Read section
✨💡
EVERYDAY ANALOGY
Everyday Metaphor: The Recipe Book and the Taste Test

You can learn to cook from a recipe book that spells out every step, or by tasting lots of dishes and adjusting until it is right. AI can be built either way.

The first way is rule-based AI. Experts write down what they know as rules, such as "if the temperature is above 38°C and there is a rash, suggest a doctor's visit". It is predictable and easy to check, but someone has to think of every case in advance.

The second way is machine learning. Instead of rules, the system is given many examples with the right answers and learns the pattern itself. It handles messy, varied situations far better, but it can be harder to explain why it gave a particular answer.

Many real products combine both: learned patterns for the messy parts, firm rules for the parts that must never go wrong.

Everyday Metaphor: The Weather of Ideas

AI has had sunny spells of excitement and long cold winters when funding dried up. Today's boom is the warmest yet, powered by data and fast chips.

AI research began in the 1950s with big promises. Early systems used rules and did well at puzzles and games, then struggled with the messy real world. Twice, disappointed funders pulled back, periods now called AI winters.

Three things changed in the 2010s: the internet produced huge amounts of example data, graphics chips made training fast, and better learning methods made use of both. Since then, machine learning, and especially neural networks, has driven most progress, from photo recognition to chat assistants.

EVERYDAY ANALOGY
Everyday Metaphor: The Office Procedures Manual

Every workplace has written procedures: if a customer asks for a refund within 30 days, approve it. Rule-based AI turns that kind of written knowledge into something a computer can follow.

Symbolic AI represents knowledge with symbols a person can read: facts like "a penguin is a bird" and rules like "if a bird cannot fly, do not suggest flying as a way to escape". The computer combines them to reach conclusions.

How you write knowledge down matters. Simple rules work for narrow tasks. For richer subjects, people use structures that link concepts together, so the computer can follow the connections. Either way, every piece of knowledge was put there by someone, which makes the system transparent but laborious to build.

📊 FACTS PLUS RULES GIVE CONCLUSIONS

Fact: penguins cannot fly

EVERYDAY ANALOGY
Everyday Metaphor: The Tiled Floor

Stand close to a tiled floor and you see individual tiles. Step back and you see the pattern. A digital photo is a floor of tiny tiles, and a computer only ever sees the tiles.

Everyday Metaphor: The Mystery Shopper

Retailers send mystery shoppers to see whether every customer gets the same service. A fairness audit sends many test cases through an AI system to see whether every group gets the same treatment.

A fairness audit compares outcomes across groups. A common check is the selection rate: what share of each group gets a yes. If one group's rate is far below another's, that is a warning sign. A widely used rule of thumb flags a problem when one group's rate is under 80% of the highest group's.

Fixes include collecting more representative data, removing or reducing proxies, adjusting how decisions are made, and then auditing again. Fairness is checked repeatedly, not once.

Everyday Metaphor: The Rejected Application

If your loan is refused, you want to know why, and what you could change. "The computer said no" is not an acceptable answer.

Many powerful models, especially large neural networks, are a black box: their decision comes from millions of learned numbers, with no simple reason to point to.

Explainability methods help. They can show which inputs mattered most for a decision, for example that income and existing debt drove a credit decision, while age did not. People affected by important decisions often have a right to a meaningful explanation, and organisations need explanations to spot errors and bias.

EVERYDAY ANALOGY
Everyday Metaphor: The Co-Pilot

Modern aircraft can largely fly themselves, but a qualified pilot stays responsible and can take over at any moment. AI used for serious decisions needs the same arrangement.

For high-stakes decisions, organisations keep a human in the loop: a qualified person reviews the AI's recommendation, can override it, and is accountable for the result.

Most responsible AI frameworks share a similar set of principles: fairness, reliability and safety, privacy and security, inclusiveness, transparency, and accountability. In practice that means testing before launch, monitoring after, protecting personal data, documenting what a system is for and how it was built, and naming who answers for it when it goes wrong.
